Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Evooo1Bot loader download cradle (wget.sh / wget||curl pipe-to-shell into /tmp) · [LLM] Evooo1Bot persistence: 5-min cron re-download & 'Apache HTTPD Cache Manager' systemd masquerade · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Evooo1Bot C2/loader traffic to relay host 91.92.40.118 · [LLM] Evooo1Bot SOCKS5 relay listener on TCP 1080 from a /tmp-resident binary · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Evooo1Bot credential sniffer artifact (/tmp/.sniff.log capture file)
Evooo1Bot C2/loader traffic to relay host 91.92.40.118 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections to the confirmed Evooo1Bot infrastructure host 91.92.40.118, which serves the /wget.sh loader and receives encrypted C2 over TCP 443. Any internal device beaconing to this IP indicates an Evooo1Bot infection of an internet-facing gateway/Linux host. Rationale: Anchored on the C2/loader IP 91.92.40.118, independently confirmed by FortiGuard Labs (hosts /wget.sh) and The Hacker News; a dedicated malicious host with no legitimate traffic, so a single hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/evooo1bot-linux-botnet-exploits-known.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-evooo1bot-linux-botnet-turns-routers-into-traffic-relay-nodes/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sandbox/detonation appliance intentionally reaching the IP during sample analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment or scanning tooling (e.g. Shodan/Censys collectors) touching the host
  • Security researcher workstation validating IOCs
  • Firewall block events (DeviceAction=deny) representing prevented, not successful, connections
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "ConnectionFailed"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source device/host and the initiating process; confirm whether the connection succeeded (allowed) vs was blocked at the firewall. 2) Contain: block 91.92.40.118 at the perimeter, isolate the source device (especially internet-facing routers/IoT), and pull the running binary for hashing. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for /tmp-resident ELF binaries, /tmp/.sniff.log, the 5-min cron re-download, and any SOCKS5 listener on 1080; sweep the fleet for other hosts contacting the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "91.92.40.118"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "91.92.40.118" or SourceIP == "91.92.40.118"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot loader download cradle (wget.sh / wget||curl pipe-to-shell into /tmp) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Evooo1Bot loader behaviour: wget, busybox wget, curl or tftp retrieving the CPU-architecture-matched binary from 91.92.40.118/wget.sh, using a `wget -qO- || curl -sL` fallback cradle, writing to a temporary path, chmod +x, and executing. Survives C2-IP rotation by also matching the structural cradle pattern. Rationale: Uses the confirmed loader URL 91.92.40.118/wget.sh plus the malware's signature `wget -qO- || curl -sL` fallback cradle documented by FortiGuard; the cradle clause catches the loader even after IP rotation while the IP/URL clause stays high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/evooo1bot-linux-botnet-exploits-known.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate install one-liners piping wget/curl to a shell (Docker convenience script, nvm, rustup, oh-my-zsh)
  • CI/CD provisioning jobs bootstrapping tooling into /tmp
  • Config-management tasks that download and chmod helper binaries
  • Admin ad-hoc troubleshooting downloading a script to /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("get.docker.com","raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh","sh.rustup.rs","install.ohmyz.sh") and not (ProcessCommandLine contains "91.92.40.118" or ProcessCommandLine contains "/wget.sh"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line and the download URL/host; the 91.92.40.118 or /wget.sh clause is malicious on sight, while a bare wget||curl cradle needs the destination checked against known provisioning sources. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and capture the /tmp binary + hash before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on persistence (5-min cron, systemd 'Apache HTTPD Cache Manager' unit), /tmp/.sniff.log, and outbound 443 to 91.92.40.118.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","wget","curl","tftp","busybox")
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "91.92.40.118"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "/wget.sh"
    or (ProcessCommandLine contains "wget -qO-" and ProcessCommandLine contains "curl -sL")
    or ((ProcessCommandLine contains "wget " or ProcessCommandLine contains "curl " or ProcessCommandLine contains "tftp ") and ProcessCommandLine contains "/tmp/" and ProcessCommandLine contains "chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine contains "91.92.40.118"
    or TargetProcessCommandLine contains "/wget.sh"
    or (TargetProcessCommandLine contains "wget -qO-" and TargetProcessCommandLine contains "curl -sL")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot persistence: 5-min cron re-download & 'Apache HTTPD Cache Manager' systemd masquerade AIInstallation High
Hunts Evooo1Bot's multi-vector persistence install: a */5 cron entry re-downloading the payload via `wget -qO- || curl -sL` every five minutes, a systemd unit masquerading as `Description=Apache HTTPD Cache Manager` with Restart=always, and download-to-shell writes into /etc/rc.local, /etc/init.d/, /etc/profile.d/. These strings are unique to the family. Rationale: Built on family-unique strings from FortiGuard: the fake systemd description 'Apache HTTPD Cache Manager' (Apache's real unit describes itself differently) and the */5 cron `wget -qO- || curl -sL` re-download cradle, both extremely rare in benign automation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-evooo1bot-linux-botnet-turns-routers-into-traffic-relay-nodes/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002 T1037.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cron jobs that fetch content with wget, but rarely with a curl fallback in the same line
  • Config management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) creating systemd units or writing rc.local
  • Monitoring agents that self-heal via cron re-download
  • A genuine Apache tuning script (would not use the exact 'Apache HTTPD Cache Manager' unit description)
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump crontab (system + per-user), /etc/systemd/system, /etc/init.d, /etc/rc.local, /etc/profile.d and confirm the offending entry; the masquerade string or wget||curl cradle confirms Evooo1Bot. 2) Contain: disable/remove the cron entry, mask the fake systemd unit, isolate the host, and preserve the artifacts. 3) Hunt: the cron re-download implies a live infection — locate the /tmp ELF, /tmp/.sniff.log, SOCKS5 listener on 1080, and outbound 443 to 91.92.40.118; sweep the fleet for the same persistence strings.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","crond","anacron") and ProcessCommandLine contains "wget -qO-" and ProcessCommandLine contains "curl -sL")
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "Apache HTTPD Cache Manager"
    or ((ProcessCommandLine contains "/etc/rc.local" or ProcessCommandLine contains "/etc/init.d/" or ProcessCommandLine contains "/etc/profile.d/" or ProcessCommandLine contains "/etc/systemd/system/") and (ProcessCommandLine contains "wget" or ProcessCommandLine contains "curl"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (ProcessName in~ ("CRON","cron","crond","anacron") and SyslogMessage contains "wget -qO-" and SyslogMessage contains "curl -sL")
    or SyslogMessage contains "Apache HTTPD Cache Manager"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Evooo1Bot Persistence Install (cron re-download / systemd masquerade)

Evooo1Bot credential sniffer artifact (/tmp/.sniff.log capture file) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of /tmp/.sniff.log, the on-disk artifact of Evooo1Bot's credential sniffer that monitors /proc/net/tcp and captures HTTP Basic Authorization and Cookie headers. The dotfile path and name are unique to this malware and constitute a direct infection artifact. Rationale: The exact path /tmp/.sniff.log is a family-unique on-disk artifact of the sniffer module documented by FortiGuard; a hidden capture log in /tmp has essentially no benign analogue, giving a near-zero FP direct hit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot
ATT&CKT1040 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin manually running tcpdump/tshark and coincidentally redirecting output to a file named .sniff.log
  • A homegrown packet-capture script that writes /tmp/.sniff.log
  • Security tooling that stages a similarly named debug log (rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tcpdump","tshark","dumpcap")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess writing /tmp/.sniff.log and its folder path (expect a /tmp-resident ELF); read the file to confirm captured Authorization/Cookie header material. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and preserve the sniffer process/binary, and treat any credentials/session cookies seen on that host's traffic as compromised — force rotation. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating binary hash and check for the cron persistence, the SOCKS5 1080 listener, and 443 C2 to 91.92.40.118 across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ ".sniff.log" or FolderPath =~ "/tmp/.sniff.log"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/tmp/.sniff.log" or TargetFileName =~ ".sniff.log"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot SOCKS5 relay listener on TCP 1080 from a /tmp-resident binary AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Evooo1Bot SOCKS5 relay module in direct-listen mode: a process running from /tmp, /dev/shm or /var/tmp opening a listener on TCP 1080 to relay attacker traffic through the compromised device. Scopes to non-standard binary locations to separate it from legitimate SOCKS proxies. Rationale: Combines the family's documented SOCKS5 default listen port 1080 (confirmed by FortiGuard/BleepingComputer) with execution from ephemeral directories (/tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp), where legitimate proxy daemons never live — turning a noisy port into a high-signal pair. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-evooo1bot-linux-botnet-turns-routers-into-traffic-relay-nodes/
ATT&CKT1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Ports
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a SOCKS proxy binary (e.g. microsocks, gost) staged in /tmp for testing
  • CI/build agents launching a temporary proxy from a scratch dir
  • Penetration-test tooling opening a 1080 pivot listener during an authorized engagement
  • ssh -D dynamic port-forward configured on 1080 (process would be sshd, not /tmp — excluded by the path filter)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","microsocks","gost","danted")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the listening binary's path and hash; a /tmp-resident ELF listening on 1080 with no package ownership is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the listener, block inbound 1080, and capture the binary; assume the device has been relaying third-party traffic. 3) Hunt: correlate with 443 C2 to 91.92.40.118, the cron persistence, and /tmp/.sniff.log; review who connected inbound to 1080 to scope downstream relayed activity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort == 1080
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 1080 and NetworkDirection == "Inbound"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkDirection, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or SHA1 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or MD5 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or SHA1 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or MD5 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SAP Commerce Cloud CVE-2026-58231: default OAuth client abuse against Data Hub Adapter AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP access to the SAP Commerce authorization-server token endpoint and the Data Hub Adapter context root from external sources, the entry vector for CVE-2026-58231 where a retained sample OAuth2 client with publicly documented credentials is abused to mint a valid token and reach vulnerable Data Hub Adapter functions. Article/CVE-specific because it pivots on the exact SAP Commerce 2211 paths (/authorizationserver/oauth/token, /datahubadapter) rather than a generic web-attack template. Rationale: Uses the concrete SAP Commerce 2211 paths confirmed across NVD/BleepingComputer/SecurityWeek writeups: the authorization-server token endpoint (default sample OAuth2 client abuse) and the /datahubadapter Data Hub Adapter context root named as the vulnerable component. External-only + these exact paths keeps it CVE-specific. defender_kql omitted: SAP Commerce web-tier URL access is not present in Defender Advanced Hunting tables (no inbound HTTP URL telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58231 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-sap-commerce-cloud-flaw-now-targeted-in-attacks/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197244/security/sap-commerce-cloud-cve-2026-58231-exploited-in-the-wild.html • https://www.securityweek.com/critical-sap-commerce-cloud-vulnerability-exploited-3-days-after-disclosure/ • https://socradar.io/blog/sap-commerce-cloud-cve-2026-58231/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Data Hub server calling the Data Hub Adapter over OAuth for scheduled data loads (internal source IP — filtered by the private-IP exclusion)
  • Uptime/health-check monitors probing /authorizationserver or /datahubadapter
  • Genuine OCC/storefront clients requesting tokens at /authorizationserver/oauth/token
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Nessus) fingerprinting the SAP Commerce authorization server
  • Partner integrations authenticating with their own (non-sample) OAuth client from an allowlisted external IP
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request(s) for the flagged SourceIP — inspect the token request body/params for the well-known SAP sample client_id and grant_type=client_credentials/password, and confirm whether a 200 (token issued) followed. Check whether the same IP then hit /datahubadapter functions. 2) Contain: apply the Onapsis workaround — configure an SAP Commerce IP Filter Set to restrict the vulnerable endpoint to trusted ranges, and confirm the environment is patched per SAP Security Note 3771065 (fixed 2211 release, rebuilt/redeployed). Rotate/disable any retained sample OAuth2 clients. 3) Hunt: if a token was issued, pivot to UC 'SAP Commerce Java process spawning a shell' on the same host and review Data Hub Adapter data read/modify activity and outbound connections from the platform node.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/authorizationserver/oauth/token", "/datahubadapter", "/datahub-webapp")
| where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","GET")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))   // external callers only; internal Data Hub->Adapter integration is legit
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(RequestMethod,10), URLs=make_set(RequestURL,25), UserAgents=make_set(RequestClientApplication,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceProduct
| order by Requests desc

SAP Commerce (Hybris) Java process spawning OS command shell — CVE-2026-58231 RCE payoff AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the arbitrary-code-execution stage of CVE-2026-58231: the SAP Commerce/Hybris platform Java process (identified by hybris/commerce/tomcat/datahub in its path or command line) spawning cmd/powershell or a Unix shell/LOLBin. A Java application server launching an interactive interpreter is the classic post-exploitation signal for this unauthenticated RCE and is distinct from generic Office-spawns-script logic. Rationale: Targets the confirmed RCE outcome of CVE-2026-58231 by anchoring on the SAP Commerce/Hybris Java platform process (path/cmdline tokens hybris, commerce, tomcat, datahub, platform) as the parent — a Java app server spawning cmd/powershell/sh is a high-fidelity webshell/RCE indicator that ties directly to the Data Hub Adapter code-execution described by Onapsis and NVD. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58231 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-sap-commerce-cloud-flaw-now-targeted-in-attacks/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197244/security/sap-commerce-cloud-cve-2026-58231-exploited-in-the-wild.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SAP Commerce media conversion / image processing where the platform shells out to ImageMagick or similar
  • Hybris build/initialize/update jobs invoking ant or shell scripts (java -> sh) during deployment
  • Solr indexing or backup/maintenance cron wrappers launched by the platform JVM
  • Admin-driven `hac`/console operations that legitimately execute OS commands
  • APM/monitoring agents attached to the JVM spawning helper shells (whoami/id health probes)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/sh -c","reverse","base64","curl ","wget ","bash -i","/dev/tcp","whoami"," id","nc ","python -c") or FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine — benign SAP activity looks like ant/initialize/imagemagick/solr; malicious looks like reverse-shell one-liners, base64, curl|wget to external IPs, or recon (whoami/id). Correlate the host and time against UC 'default OAuth client abuse' web hits. 2) Contain: isolate the SAP Commerce node, capture the process tree and any dropped files, and block outbound to any C2 IP the shell contacted; confirm the deployment is on the fixed 2211 build per SAP Security Note 3771065. 3) Hunt: sweep other Commerce/Hybris nodes for the same java->shell pattern, review Data Hub Adapter data access, new local accounts, cron/systemd or scheduled-task persistence, and outbound connections from the platform service account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","java.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hybris","commerce","tomcat","datahub","platform") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("hybris","commerce","tomcat")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","python","python3","perl","curl","wget","whoami","id","busybox")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java","java.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hybris","commerce","tomcat","datahub","platform")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","/sh","dash","python","python3","perl","curl","wget","whoami","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

A recently patched security flaw in Apple macOS has come under active exploitation in the wild to deploy a cryptocurrency miner, the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) has warned. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-65400 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical authentication issue impacting the Screen Sharing component that could allow an attacker already on the network to

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internet-facing macOS hosts unpatched against the Screen Sharing CVE cluster (exposure hunt) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound Screen Sharing (VNC port 5900) from a public IP to a Mac — CVE-2026-65400 exposure · [LLM] macOS screensharingd spawning a shell or downloader as root (post-exploit RCE) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Attacker-controlled sudoers policy written under /etc/sudoers.d (CVE-2026-43760 root file-create primitive)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Monero (XMRig) mining pool egress from a macOS host post-Screen-Sharing compromise · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Inbound Screen Sharing (VNC port 5900) from a public IP to a Mac — CVE-2026-65400 exposure AIExploitation Medium
Hunts internet-sourced inbound connections to the macOS Screen Sharing daemon (screensharingd) on TCP/5900, the exact exposure NCSC-NL reported being abused to pre-auth-bypass CVE-2026-65400 and gain root. Surfaces the attack surface (~40k exposed hosts per @osxreverser) and live exploitation attempts. Rationale: Uses the exact exposed service (screensharingd/TCP 5900) and public-source constraint from the NCSC-NL report; port 5900 + internet-source is the precondition every confirmed compromise shared. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macos-screen-sharing-rce-patched • https://www.securityweek.com/recent-macos-screen-sharing-vulnerability-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/bugs/2026/08/update-your-mac-screen-sharing-vulnerability-exploited-in-the-wild
ATT&CKT1190 T1021.005 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote admin using Apple Remote Desktop / Screen Sharing over the internet without a VPN
  • MSP/support tooling that connects to Macs over 5900 through a NAT/port-forward
  • Internet scanning services (Shodan/Censys) probing 5900 — will show as accepted then reset
  • Home users intentionally exposing Screen Sharing for personal remote access
  • Load-balancer/health-check probes on 5900 for a screen-share gateway
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<known-admin-jump-hosts>") // maintain an allowlist of sanctioned remote-admin source IPs; prefer removing internet exposure entirely
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Mac is genuinely internet-exposed on 5900 and check its macOS build against patched versions (Tahoe 26.6.1 / Sequoia 15.7.9 / Sonoma 14.8.9); geolocate RemoteIP and check reputation. 2) Contain: block inbound 5900 at the perimeter/host firewall and disable Screen Sharing (General > Sharing) on the host immediately; if unpatched, treat as presumed-compromised. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to screensharingd child processes (UC2), /etc/sudoers.d writes (UC3), and Monero pool egress (UC4) to confirm post-exploitation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 5900
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("screensharingd","AppleVNCServer","ARDAgent")
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 5900
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, SrcIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by LastSeen desc

macOS screensharingd spawning a shell or downloader as root (post-exploit RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects the Screen Sharing daemon (screensharingd) or its file-copy helpers spawning a shell, scripting, or download utility — the remote-root code execution primitive delivered by CVE-2026-65400 / CVE-2026-43760. screensharingd legitimately never launches bash/curl/python, so a child of this shape is high-fidelity post-exploitation. Rationale: Parent=screensharingd (or the named SSFileCopyReceiver/Sender helpers from the Huntress breakdown) spawning a shell/downloader is the exact RCE primitive; this parent never legitimately spawns these binaries, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macos-screen-sharing-rce-patched • https://cybersecuritynews.com/apple-screen-sharing-vulnerability/amp/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1021.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Apple diagnostics or MDM (Jamf) invoking helper scripts under a screen-share session (rare, verify signature)
  • Security testers/red team validating CVE-2026-65400 in a lab
  • Screen-share-assisted admin manually running a shell during a support session (child should be a Terminal GUI, not a direct curl/python child of screensharingd)
  • macOS beta telemetry mislabeling the daemon's own helper spawns
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "jamf" and InitiatingProcessAccountName != "_mbsetupuser"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and command line — inspect what the shell/curl fetched and where it wrote; confirm the host is unpatched and 5900 is exposed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child chain, disable Screen Sharing, and rotate any credentials the process could reach; snapshot for forensics. 3) Hunt: check /etc/sudoers.d for attacker-planted policy (UC3), LaunchDaemons/LaunchAgents for persistence, and outbound Monero pool traffic (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("screensharingd","SSFileCopyReceiver","SSFileCopySender")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","curl","wget","osascript","python","python3","perl","chmod","launchctl","dscl","tee","nohup")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("screensharingd","SSFileCopyReceiver","SSFileCopySender")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/bash","/sh","/zsh","/curl","/wget","/osascript","/python","/python3","/perl","/chmod","/launchctl","/dscl","/tee","/nohup")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker-controlled sudoers policy written under /etc/sudoers.d (CVE-2026-43760 root file-create primitive) AIInstallation High
Detects file creation/modification under /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers on macOS — the exact LPE-to-remote-root primitive Pesoli described, where the Screen Sharing file-copy helper is coerced into installing a valid sudoers policy as root. A non-visudo, non-MDM process writing here is a strong privilege-escalation signal. Rationale: Targets the precise post-exploit action Pesoli documented — 'install a valid sudoers policy' via the file-copy primitive — anchored on the /etc/sudoers.d path; legitimate writers are limited to visudo and a few MDM agents, which are filtered. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macos-screen-sharing-rce-patched • https://cybersecuritynews.com/apple-screen-sharing-vulnerability/amp/
ATT&CKT1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Jamf/Munki/Chef/Ansible deploying an admin sudoers drop-in for privileged automation
  • Homebrew or developer tooling adding a NOPASSWD entry for a service account
  • macOS admin manually editing sudoers via visudo (filtered) or a text editor
  • VPN/EDR agent installers writing their own sudoers policy at deploy time
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jamf","munki","managedsoftwareupdate","chef-client","ansible","brew") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "MDM"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the written sudoers file — a policy granting NOPASSWD/ALL to an unexpected user is confirmation; correlate the writing process (should not be screensharingd or a copy helper) and timestamp against 5900 inbound activity. 2) Contain: remove the malicious sudoers drop-in, isolate the host, disable Screen Sharing, and audit /etc/sudoers.d for other entries; force-patch macOS. 3) Hunt: check for the account named in the policy authenticating, new LaunchDaemons, and Monero miner egress (UC4).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/sudoers.d","/private/etc/sudoers.d") or FolderPath in~ ("/etc/sudoers","/private/etc/sudoers")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("visudo","sudo")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/sudoers.d","/private/etc/sudoers.d") or TargetFilePath in~ ("/etc/sudoers","/private/etc/sudoers")
| where ActingProcessName !has "visudo"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Monero (XMRig) mining pool egress from a macOS host post-Screen-Sharing compromise AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects macOS endpoints connecting to known Monero mining pools or stratum mining ports — the payload NCSC-NL reported dropped as root in every confirmed CVE-2026-65400 compromise. Scoped to macOS devices to keep it campaign-specific rather than a generic cryptojacking template. Rationale: Ties the article's stated payload (Monero miner installed as root) to macOS-scoped egress toward well-known Monero pool domains/stratum ports; pool-domain matches are high-fidelity, port-only matches are the noisier hunting tail. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/197234/uncategorized/macos-screen-sharing-flaw-exploited-to-deploy-monero-miners.html • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/hotforsecurity/macos-screen-sharing-flaw-exploited-crypto-miner-hack
ATT&CKT1496
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/researcher running a legitimate XMRig benchmark or joining a pool intentionally on their Mac
  • Enterprise app using ports 3333/4444/7777 for a non-mining service (some proxies, Redis clusters, game servers)
  • Threat-intel/sandbox host deliberately detonating the miner
  • Blockchain/crypto engineering team connecting to pool infrastructure as part of their job
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Applications/" and InitiatingProcessAccountName != "<sanctioned-crypto-dev-user>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/folder and account (a root-owned binary in /tmp, /Users/Shared, or /Library is confirmation); check CPU/thermals and whether the host had inbound 5900. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the miner binary and its LaunchDaemon/LaunchAgent, block the pool domains/IPs, and rebuild if root was obtained via the exploit. 3) Hunt: sweep all macOS hosts for the same pool destinations and for screensharingd child processes / sudoers writes to find other compromised Macs.
let macs = DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where OSPlatform =~ "macOS" | distinct DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceId in (macs)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any ("supportxmr","moneroocean","xmrpool","2miners","monerohash","nanopool","hashvault","c3pool","minexmr"))
     or (RemotePort in (3333,4444,5555,7777,9000,14433,14444,45560,45700) and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("supportxmr","moneroocean","xmrpool","2miners","monerohash","nanopool","hashvault","c3pool","minexmr")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing macOS hosts unpatched against the Screen Sharing CVE cluster (exposure hunt) AIReconnaissance High
Identifies managed Macs that are both internet-facing and still vulnerable to the Screen Sharing flaws (CVE-2026-65400 and the CVE-2026-4377x cluster) fixed in Tahoe 26.6.1 / Sequoia 15.7.9 / Sonoma 14.8.9. This is the prioritized patch/attack-surface list — the fastest way to shrink exposure before exploitation. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE IDs and the patched-version facts from the article/Apple advisory joined to IsInternetFacing to produce an actionable, host-level exposure list — the exact population NCSC-NL says is being hit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/recent-macos-screen-sharing-vulnerability-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/bugs/2026/08/update-your-mac-screen-sharing-vulnerability-exploited-in-the-wild
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IsInternetFacing inferred from a NATed public IP shared by many internal hosts (device may not truly expose 5900)
  • TVM catalog lag — device patched to 26.6.1/15.7.9/14.8.9 but not yet rescanned still shows the CVE
  • Devices that have Screen Sharing disabled entirely (vulnerable build but no reachable service)
  • Decommissioned/duplicate DeviceId entries inflating the exposed count
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate each host's actual macOS build and whether 5900 is truly reachable from outside (correlate with UC1 inbound hits). 2) Contain: push emergency patch to Tahoe 26.6.1 / Sequoia 15.7.9 / Sonoma 14.8.9, or disable Screen Sharing where patching is delayed; block 5900 at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: for any host that was both exposed and unpatched, run UC2/UC3/UC4 retroactively to rule out prior compromise before closing.

| where OSPlatform =~ "macOS"
| where IsInternetFacing == true
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, PublicIP, OSVersion;
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-65400","CVE-2026-43760","CVE-2026-43779","CVE-2026-43777")
| join kind=inner exposed on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, PublicIP, OSVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by CveId asc

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Top enterprise SCA tools in 2026
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

let BadHashes = dynamic(["9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "927387d0cfac1118df4b383decc2ea6ba49c9d2f98b47098bcbcba1efc026e1f", "14eb4ce01dd4307759887ff819359b70d7d9ff709ecde039a5abc1aac325b128", "3f3f42d072bd36860ab7bd7fb5e10ac0d22c741c13c89505ccd6ec0ea572eea7", "29ac906c8bd801dfe1cb39596197df49f80fff2270b3e7fbab52287c24e4f1a7", "619c56acf572df75b6004a6fc013c80900316a76099b241d64312da3a44f10b4"]);
union

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,

                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Execution/write of published Sable Squirrel malware sample (SHA256 0464caa1...) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint callback to Sable Squirrel dropcatch C2 domains (Quasar RAT via cel-robox[.]com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Endpoint callback to Sable Squirrel dropcatch C2 domains (Quasar RAT via cel-robox[.]com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network callbacks to the specific expired 'dropcatch' domains re-registered by Sable Squirrel that double as RAT command-and-control (cel-robox[.]com serves Quasar RAT C2 while still presenting streaming content). Non-browser process reaching these aged-reputation domains is high-fidelity RAT beaconing, not a user visiting a stream. Rationale: Uses the 20 concrete Sable Squirrel dropcatch domains from the article/IOC set — including cel-robox[.]com which Infoblox confirms is a live Quasar RAT C2 — cross-checked against Infoblox's own blog. Non-browser initiating-process filter on the endpoint variant separates RAT beaconing from users merely watching the illegal stream. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/7-million-in-expired-domains-fuel-a-streaming-empire-with-a-malware-secret/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197251/cyber-crime/crooks-are-buying-your-expired-domains-and-using-them-to-deliver-malware.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/cybercriminals-invest-millions-in-expired-domains-for-illicit-activities
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately visiting one of the illegal sports-streaming front-ends (Xoilac/Cakhia branded) in a browser — mitigated by the non-browser process filter on the endpoint query
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliances resolving the IOCs for research
  • Security scanners or DNS-sinkhole resolvers querying the domains for reputation checks
  • A previous benign owner's cached CNAME/record still resolving (e.g. GE healthymagination legacy links) from an old bookmark
  • Corporate web proxy pre-fetching link previews of the domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","safari.exe","MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the host that resolved/connected to the domain. If it is a browser and only DNS (no non-browser process), likely a stream visit; if it is a non-browser binary (rundll32, a random-named exe, scripting host), treat as RAT beacon and pull the process tree + SHA256. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block all 20 domains at the proxy/DNS firewall, and quarantine the initiating binary. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same domains org-wide and for the published sample hash (see companion UC); check for Quasar/AsyncRAT/DCRat persistence (Run keys, scheduled tasks) and additional dropcatch domains resolving from the same host.

Execution/write of published Sable Squirrel malware sample (SHA256 0464caa1...) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or drop of the specific malware sample Infoblox published as communicating with Sable Squirrel C2 infrastructure, identified by its SHA256. A direct hash match on any endpoint is an unambiguous confirmed-infection signal for this campaign. Rationale: Direct match on the single SHA256 (0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216) Infoblox tied to Sable Squirrel C2 traffic — a hash match is zero-ambiguity confirmed infection and pairs with the domain callback UC for corroboration. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/7-million-in-expired-domains-fuel-a-streaming-empire-with-a-malware-secret/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hackers-spend-nearly-7-million-on.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or IR team detonating the sample in an on-network sandbox VM that reports to the EDR/SIEM
  • Security researcher storing the IOC sample in a quarantined evidence share that gets hash-scanned
  • AV/EDR itself quarantining and re-hashing the file (may surface as a file event)
  • Threat-intel platform syncing the sample into a local malware zoo appliance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash match is on a production endpoint (not a sanctioned sandbox/evidence host); capture the full process tree, parent process, file path, and originating download URL. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine/kill the sample, and block the 20 Sable Squirrel domains (companion UC) at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound connections for callbacks to Sable Squirrel domains and other Quasar/AsyncRAT/DCRat/njRAT indicators; check persistence (Run keys, scheduled tasks, services) and sweep the org for the same hash and any sibling samples dropped in the same folder.
let TargetSHA256 = "0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216";
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA256 == TargetSHA256 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="ProcessExec", AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256),
  (DeviceFileEvents  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA256 == TargetSHA256 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
let TargetSHA256 = "0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where SHA256 =~ TargetSHA256 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256),
  (ImFileEvent    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where TargetFileSHA256 =~ TargetSHA256 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216") or SHA1 in~ ("0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216") or MD5 in~ ("0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216") or SHA1 in~ ("0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216") or MD5 in~ ("0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0464caa1c45cb753db25a95a30ce0b6814650b6f839a07cf8c2afdc143de7216"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
