HoneyMyte DLL side-load: renamed Sangfor 'defender.exe' loading malicious libngs.dll AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CoolClient first-stage loader where a legitimate Sangfor binary renamed to defender.exe (masquerading as Windows Defender) side-loads a malicious libngs.dll to decrypt and run loadcert.ini. Pivots on the article's exact DLL name and both published libngs.dll MD5s. Rationale: Uses the article's exact first-stage DLL name (libngs.dll), both published MD5s, and the masqueraded parent defender.exe (a renamed Sangfor Sang.exe) — all confirmed by Kaspersky/Securelist and Security Affairs. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197274/apt/mustang-panda-upgrades-coolclient-with-a-kernel-rootkit.html • https://gbhackers.com/honeymyte-upgrades-coolclient/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Sangfor endpoint agent installed under its real product path loading its own libngs.dll (verify signer/path)
  • Third-party security software that legitimately ships a binary named defender.exe
  • Sysmon image-load noise from software update staging directories
  • Hash reuse in a malware sandbox/detonation VM generating benign-looking loads
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Windows Defender" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Sangfor\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading process is named defender.exe but resides OUTSIDE %ProgramFiles%\Windows Defender (e.g. a fake Microsoft\Windows Defender folder) and that libngs.dll is unsigned or Sangfor-signed in a non-Sangfor path; pull the SHA256 and check the parent scheduled task. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the defender.exe process tree, and quarantine libngs.dll, loadcert.ini, cert.ini, time.ini in that directory. 3) Hunt: search for msagent.sys, the msagent/media_updaten services, the goopdate Run value, and injection into synchost.exe on this and peer hosts.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "defender.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "libngs.dll"

CoolClient signed kernel rootkit msagent.sys dropped and registered as 'msagent' driver service AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CoolClient rootkit driver: loadcert.ini extracts an LZMA-compressed kernel driver to disk as msagent.sys (signed with the revoked Nanjing Ranyi cert) and starts it as a driver service named msagent. Pivots on the exact filename, both published MD5s, and the service name. Rationale: msagent.sys, both driver MD5s, and the 'msagent' driver-service name are the article's highest-fidelity kernel-rootkit artifacts; a .sys kernel driver named msagent (distinct from legacy user-mode Microsoft Agent) is unambiguous. Confirmed by Securelist and BetaNews. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://betanews.com/article/honeymyte-coolclient-kernel-rootkit/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197274/apt/mustang-panda-upgrades-coolclient-with-a-kernel-rootkit.html
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003 T1553.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy third-party product legitimately naming a service 'msagent' (rare; verify it is a kernel .sys driver)
  • EDR/AV sample-analysis VM detonating the known-bad hashes
  • Restore of an old backup image that contains a quarantined msagent.sys copy
  • Manual IR collection copying msagent.sys to an evidence share (initiating process = forensic tool)
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the file is a kernel-mode driver (.sys) and whether it is signed by 'Nanjing Ranyi Technology Co., Ltd.'; capture the SHA256 and the initiating process (expect loadcert.ini logic hosted by defender.exe). 2) Contain: isolate the host; the rootkit protects its own process/files, so collect memory before attempting deletion and stop/disable the msagent service from a clean boot/PE environment. 3) Hunt: enumerate HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services for msagent and media_updaten, look for HKLM\SYSTEM\RNG rootkit config, and sweep the fleet for the two msagent.sys MD5s and the Nanjing Ranyi code-signing cert.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msagent.sys"
    or MD5 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63","9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName =~ "msagent" or ServiceFileName has "msagent.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CoolClient persistence: 'goopdate' Run key and 'media_updaten' service creation AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CoolClient's second-stage persistence: an AutoRun value named goopdate (masquerading as Google Update) and/or a Windows service named media_updaten. Both names are taken verbatim from Kaspersky's write-up. Rationale: goopdate and media_updaten are the exact persistence names Kaspersky documented for this CoolClient variant; the GoogleUpdate.exe exclusion strips the main goopdate.dll masquerade false positive while keeping the unusual value/service names in scope. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://gbhackers.com/honeymyte-upgrades-coolclient/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Google Update writing a goopdate-named autorun value (filtered by GoogleUpdate.exe exclusion)
  • Software packaging tools that create oddly-named media/update services during install
  • Admin-authored scheduled maintenance service with a similar name
  • Backup/imaging agents re-writing Run keys on restore
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueName =~ "goopdate" and RegistryValueData has_cs "GoogleUpdate.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RegistryValueData/ServiceFileName behind goopdate and media_updaten — legitimate Google Update points to GoogleUpdate.exe under Program Files; malicious points to defender.exe or the fake Windows Defender directory. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the media_updaten service and delete the goopdate Run value, then remove the scheduled task launching defender.exe as SYSTEM. 3) Hunt: correlate to msagent.sys / msagent service and libngs.dll on the same host and pivot the fleet on the media_updaten service name.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RegistryKey has @"\Services\media_updaten")
    or (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValueName =~ "goopdate")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "GoogleUpdate.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (RegistryKey has @"\Services\media_updaten")
    or (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValue =~ "goopdate")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "GoogleUpdate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PlugX adds Microsoft Defender exclusions for CoolClient components and fake Defender dir AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the PlugX pre-staging step where Defender path/process exclusions are added for the fake Windows Defender install directory, the renamed sideloading executable (defender.exe), and CoolClient components (libngs.dll, loadcert.ini, cert.ini, msagent.sys). Rationale: The exclusion targets are the article's own component filenames plus the renamed defender.exe under a fake 'Windows Defender' directory; a Defender exclusion naming these strings is not something a legitimate admin would add. Corroborated by Securelist and Security Affairs. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197274/apt/mustang-panda-upgrades-coolclient-with-a-kernel-rootkit.html
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately excluding a genuine third-party 'defender.exe' security tool from scans
  • Software vendor installer adding its own .ini/.dll exclusion during setup
  • Security testing / red-team tooling adding exclusions during an authorized exercise
  • Backup software excluding a directory that coincidentally contains an ini file
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the excluded path/process — an exclusion for defender.exe or a fake Microsoft\Windows Defender folder pointing outside %ProgramFiles% is malicious; capture the initiating process (expect PlugX/rundll32-hosted logic). 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the malicious Defender exclusions immediately, and re-run a full scan. 3) Hunt: from the excluded directory enumerate libngs.dll/loadcert.ini/cert.ini/msagent.sys, and pivot to the goopdate Run value, media_updaten service, and synchost.exe injection.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Windows Defender\Exclusions"
| where RegistryValueName has_any ("defender.exe","libngs.dll","loadcert.ini","cert.ini","msagent.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Windows Defender\Exclusions"
| where RegistryValue has_any ("defender.exe","libngs.dll","loadcert.ini","cert.ini","msagent.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CoolClient injection target: masqueraded 'synchost.exe' (svchost typosquat) execution AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of a process named synchost.exe — a masquerade of the legitimate svchost.exe — into which CoolClient injects its rootkit-protected code. No legitimate Windows binary is named synchost.exe, making its presence a high-fidelity indicator. Rationale: synchost.exe is a deliberate one-letter typosquat of svchost.exe named explicitly in Kaspersky's report as the CoolClient injection host; no legitimate Microsoft process uses this name, so bare execution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://gbhackers.com/honeymyte-upgrades-coolclient/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party 'sync host' utility legitimately named synchost.exe (verify signer/path)
  • Developer/test binary coincidentally named synchost.exe in a build output folder
  • Malware sandbox detonation of the CoolClient sample
  • Analyst renaming a sample to synchost.exe during manual analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary is named synchost.exe (not svchost.exe) and check its path, signer, and parent — legitimate svchost runs from System32 under services.exe; a rootkit-hidden synchost.exe will be unsigned and injected. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture volatile memory before termination (the msagent driver reduces open-handle rights, so use offline/PE tooling to remove it). 3) Hunt: correlate the synchost.exe host to msagent.sys, the msagent/media_updaten services, goopdate Run value, and libngs.dll; review outbound connections since the nsiproxy hook hides C2 from user mode but kernel-level EDR network telemetry may still record them.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "synchost.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "synchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\synchost.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\synchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ImFileEvent

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f") or SHA1 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f") or MD5 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f") or SHA1 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f") or MD5 in~ ("2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2d7c8780e97409770a9d4f31c66c9d63", "9460e150e1981d5c165043520c5c12fe", "9717f005c5fb98e08d2ad983d88f94ee", "f518d8e5fe70d9090f6280c68a95998f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chrome DevTools Technique Enables Authenticated Session Hijacking in Live Windows Browsers

The Hacker News
2026-08-14 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have detailed a post-exploitation technique that enables the&nbsp;Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)&nbsp;inside a running Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge process on Windows, allowing an operator to access cookies, saved data, and authenticated browser sessions. The technique assumes that an operator already has code execution on the Windows host and does not involve

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chrome DevTools Technique Enables Authenticated Session Hijacking in Live Window
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CDP-Enable-BOF: CreateRemoteThread injection into chrome.exe / msedge.exe
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Suspicious ProcessAccess to chrome.exe / msedge.exe with injection-grade rights · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
CDP-Enable-BOF: CreateRemoteThread injection into chrome.exe / msedge.exe AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a non-browser process creating a remote thread inside a live chrome.exe or msedge.exe, the injection primitive SpecterOps' CDP-Enable-BOF uses to activate Chromium's internal StartRemoteDebuggingServer from within the running browser. Article-specific because it targets injection INTO the browser process (not generic injection) with expected legitimate injectors filtered out. Rationale: The article states defenders should watch Sysmon EID 8 for process injection targeting chrome.exe/msedge.exe; this pins TargetImage to the two browser binaries and excludes the browser's own multi-process/update injectors, isolating the CDP-Enable-BOF injection primitive that precedes StartRemoteDebuggingServer. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/003/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chrome-devtools-technique-enables.html
ATT&CKT1055 T1055.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/DLP agents (e.g. Netskope, Zscaler, Forcepoint) injecting inspection threads into browsers
  • Accessibility/IME software hooking the browser UI thread
  • Browser crash-reporter or profiler tooling
  • Some password managers injecting into the renderer
  • Legitimate red-team/BAS tooling during authorized testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify SourceImage (injector) path, signer, and parent chain; confirm whether it is a sanctioned security agent. Pull the injector's SHA256 and check prevalence org-wide and against threat intel. 2) CONTAIN: If the injector is unsigned, in a user-writable path, or unknown, isolate the host and suspend/kill the injector process; preserve the browser process for memory capture before it exits. 3) HUNT: On the same host look for a listening remote-debugging port and outbound CDP/WebSocket traffic, ProcessAccess (EID 10) handle opens to the browser with VM_WRITE/CREATE_THREAD rights, and subsequent Storage.getCookies-style browser data access; sweep the fleet for the same injector hash.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","AllocateVirtualMemoryRemoteApiCall","WriteToProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","googleupdate.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessId, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 8
| extend SourceImage = extract(@'Name="SourceImage">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| extend TargetImage = extract(@'Name="TargetImage">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| extend StartFunction = extract(@'Name="StartFunction">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| where TargetImage has_any ("\\chrome.exe","\\msedge.exe")
| where SourceImage !has "chrome.exe" and SourceImage !has "msedge.exe" and SourceImage !has "msedgewebview2.exe"
| where SourceImage !has "MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe" and SourceImage !has "GoogleUpdate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceImage, TargetImage, StartFunction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CreateRemoteThread Injection Targeting Chrome or Edge (CDP-Enable-BOF)
id: 3f2a7c1e-8b44-4c9a-9e21-7d6f0a1b2c34
status: experimental
description: Detects a non-browser process creating a remote thread in chrome.exe or msedge.exe, consistent with SpecterOps CDP-Enable-BOF activating remote debugging inside a live browser.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chrome-devtools-technique-enables.html
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/18
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1055
  - attack.t1055.003
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: create_remote_thread
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
  filter_browser:
    SourceImage|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\msedgewebview2.exe'
      - '\MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe'
      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
  - Endpoint security / DLP products that inject monitoring threads into browsers
  - IME or accessibility software hooking the browser UI thread
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:8 (@TargetImage:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MsEdge.exe)) NOT (@SourceImage:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MsEdge.exe OR *\\msedgewebview2.exe OR *\\MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe))
#event_simpleName=DllInjection
| TargetImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|msedgewebview2|MicrosoftEdgeUpdate|GoogleUpdate)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
`sysmon` EventCode=8 (TargetImage="*\\chrome.exe" OR TargetImage="*\\msedge.exe")
| regex SourceImage!="(?i)\\\\(chrome|msedge|msedgewebview2|MicrosoftEdgeUpdate|GoogleUpdate)\.exe$"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(SourceImage) as SourceImage values(StartAddress) as StartAddress by Computer, TargetImage
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Suspicious ProcessAccess to chrome.exe / msedge.exe with injection-grade rights AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a non-browser process opening a handle to a live chrome.exe or msedge.exe with high access masks (VM_WRITE / VM_OPERATION / CREATE_THREAD / PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), the handle acquisition CDP-Enable-BOF needs to allocate remote memory and install a remote window procedure before calling StartRemoteDebuggingServer. Article-specific: SpecterOps names Sysmon EID 10 (ProcessAccess) as the second detection signal for this browser-session-hijack technique. Rationale: SpecterOps explicitly cites Sysmon EID 10 (ProcessAccess) alongside EID 8; the CDP-Enable-BOF steps (allocate remote memory, install remote window procedure, CreateRemoteThread) require a handle with VM_WRITE/VM_OPERATION/CREATE_THREAD, so filtering TargetImage to the two browsers plus injection-grade GrantedAccess masks isolates the handle-open that precedes session hijack while excluding the browser's own sandbox brokering. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chrome-devtools-technique-enables.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR agents opening browser handles for memory inspection (VM_READ heavy but sometimes full-access)
  • Attached debuggers or crash-dump tools (WerFault, procdump during a browser crash)
  • Enterprise DLP reading browser memory to inspect uploads
  • Performance profilers/APM agents
  • Sanctioned red-team CDP tooling in a test window
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("werfault.exe","procdump.exe","procdump64.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the GrantedAccess mask indicates write/thread rights (not read-only inspection) and identify the SourceImage signer/path; benign inspection tools are usually signed and in Program Files. 2) CONTAIN: If SourceImage is unknown/unsigned or user-writable, isolate the host, kill the SourceImage, and capture the browser process memory before termination. 3) HUNT: Correlate with a matching EID 8 CreateRemoteThread into the same browser, a newly listening remote-debugging port, and outbound WebSocket/CDP traffic; check identity logs for the affected user's session reuse from anomalous IPs (session-hijack replay) and force session/cookie revocation.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ReadProcessMemoryApiCall"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","googleupdate.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 10
| extend SourceImage = extract(@'Name="SourceImage">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| extend TargetImage = extract(@'Name="TargetImage">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| extend GrantedAccess = extract(@'Name="GrantedAccess">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| extend CallTrace = extract(@'Name="CallTrace">([^<]+)<', 1, EventData)
| where TargetImage has_any ("\\chrome.exe","\\msedge.exe")
| where GrantedAccess in~ ("0x1F0FFF","0x1F1FFF","0x1F3FFF","0x1FFFFF","0x147A","0x143A","0x1478","0x1410")
| where SourceImage !has "chrome.exe" and SourceImage !has "msedge.exe" and SourceImage !has "msedgewebview2.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess, CallTrace
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

2026-08-14 11 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a large-scale, global recruitment-themed phishing campaign that uses fake interview scheduling pages and Browser-in-the-Browser (BitB) windows to steal Google and Facebook credentials and, in more advanced cases, relay multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts in real time. CTM360, which detailed the activity in a new report titled RecruitTrap, said it

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RecruitTrap recruitment lure via abused PeopleForce (reply.peopleforce.io) ATS relay · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Browser navigation to BitB Calendly-lookalike phishing host (rare .cfd/.work TLD) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AiTM MFA-relay: successful Entra sign-in from AWS EC2 / hosting ASN · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
RecruitTrap recruitment lure via abused PeopleForce (reply.peopleforce.io) ATS relay AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound recruitment/interview-themed emails delivered through the PeopleForce transactional relay (reply.peopleforce.io) that impersonate well-known brands (e.g. McKinsey) and carry a scheduling CTA — the confirmed RecruitTrap delivery vector. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact abused sending domain and recruitment lure semantics rather than generic phishing. Rationale: Anchors on the exact abused relay reply.peopleforce.io and recruitment/scheduling lure confirmed in the article screenshot (McKinsey impersonation, 'Reviewing your digital project availability', 'VIEW CALENDAR & SCHEDULE CALL'). Cross-checked CTM360 report and the sender infra shown in image [2]. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/recruittrap-browser-in-the-browser-bitb-recruitment-scams • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiSOzmEWM2SNbhEpY-jQgfa1yCugokRuRT5h1SsLXzFkSMRgGmVchIO-_A2DbZJMsEao_3A2HbdXixdGoFEdJoEvBS9F-V7FVp2R6W9_v-8AfWJTmmIaZ19Zx2LtyESoQSCGiIh36CCeIJUA-mescurDLgf4BaT35XjEiO8U5riNZmu9i9s90T4dmFfufo/s1700-e365/1.png
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Your organisation legitimately uses PeopleForce as its ATS — genuine candidate/recruiter mail also flows from reply.peopleforce.io
  • A real third-party recruiter your staff engaged uses PeopleForce for scheduling
  • Marketing/newsletter mail routed through PeopleForce that happens to contain 'opportunity'/'availability'
  • Internal talent team forwarding a legitimate PeopleForce invite inbound
Suppression filter
| where not (RecipientEmailAddress in~ ("talent@yourco.com","hr@yourco.com")) // exclude your own HR mailboxes that legitimately transact with PeopleForce
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the sender display name/brand (e.g. McKinsey) is an org your company has NO recruiting relationship with, and inspect the CTA link destination — RecruitTrap points to Calendly-lookalike / rare-TLD hosts, not calendly.com. 2) Contain: Quarantine/soft-delete the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, block the destination host, and warn recipients not to click. 3) Hunt: Pull all recipients, check UrlClickEvents for clicks and correlate to the AiTM sign-in detection (UC3) for any recipient who reached the credential trap.

Browser navigation to BitB Calendly-lookalike phishing host (rare .cfd/.work TLD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts endpoint browsers resolving/connecting to RecruitTrap credential-trap infrastructure: Calendly-lookalike hostnames and the campaign's dominant rare TLDs (.cfd 40%, .work, .works) that are not the legitimate calendly.com. Article-specific via the confirmed TLD distribution and Calendly theme (96% of pages). Rationale: Uses the article's measured infrastructure fingerprint: .cfd is the top TLD (40%) with .work/.works, and 96% of pages spoof the Calendly theme, so a browser hitting a Calendly-lookalike host that is not calendly.com on those TLDs is high-signal. Excludes the legitimate calendly.com to preserve TP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/recruittrap-browser-in-the-browser-bitb-recruitment-scams
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate business sites that happen to use .work/.works/.cfd TLDs
  • A real vendor using a 'calendly'-branded subdomain on their own domain for embedded scheduling
  • Ad/analytics beacons resolving newly-registered .cfd domains unrelated to the campaign
  • Security researchers/threat-intel staff intentionally browsing the phishing hosts for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.work","basecamp.works")) // extend with org-approved rare-TLD business domains after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the user/device and check whether the DNS/web hit was preceded by a click on a recruitment email (UrlClickEvents / UC1 hit). Pull the full URL and screenshot the page if still live. 2) Contain: Block the host at proxy/DNS, isolate the device if a credential form was submitted, and force password + session-token reset for the user. 3) Hunt: Sweep all devices for the same host and sibling hosts on the same registrant/TLD, then pivot to UC3 to see if the relayed credentials produced a datacenter sign-in.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Host = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where Host endswith ".cfd" or Host endswith ".work" or Host endswith ".works"
    or (Host contains "calendly" and Host !endswith "calendly.com" and Host !endswith ".calendly.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Devices=dcount(DeviceName), SampleUser=any(InitiatingProcessAccountName) by RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Url).Host))
| where Host endswith ".cfd" or Host endswith ".work" or Host endswith ".works"
    or (Host contains "calendly" and Host !endswith "calendly.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Sources=dcount(SrcIpAddr), SampleUser=any(SrcUsername) by Host
| order by FirstSeen desc

AiTM MFA-relay: successful Entra sign-in from AWS EC2 / hosting ASN AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the RecruitTrap account-takeover payoff: a successful, MFA-satisfied browser sign-in originating from AWS EC2 hosting ranges/ASNs — where 50.9% of the campaign's infrastructure lives. No legitimate user interactively completes MFA from a datacenter IP, so this is the AiTM relay landing on the real identity provider. Rationale: Ties the campaign's confirmed hosting fact (50.9% AWS EC2) to the AiTM outcome: a successful MFA-satisfied browser sign-in from Amazon EC2 ASNs (14618/16509) or EC2 CIDRs is behaviourally impossible for a real user and is the token-relay landing. Cross-checked Microsoft Sentinel AiTM guidance, Elastic Tycoon-2FA AiTM detection, and Datadog's AWS AiTM writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/recruittrap-browser-in-the-browser-bitb-recruitment-scams • https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftsentinelblog/detecting-aitm-phishing-via-3rd-party-network-events-in-unified-security-operati/4224653 • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/tycoon-2fa-aitm-detection-engineering • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/behind-the-console-aws-aitm-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1557 T1111 T1078.004 T1550.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A service account or automation legitimately authenticating to Entra from an EC2-hosted workload (CI/CD, backup, monitoring)
  • A corporate VPN/SASE egress or cloud-hosted secure web gateway that terminates on AWS
  • A penetration test / red-team sign-in launched from AWS infrastructure
  • A developer using a cloud-hosted browser or remote dev box on EC2
Suppression filter
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$" and AppDisplayName !in~ ("Azure DevOps","GitHub Actions") // exclude known EC2-hosted automation apps after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the UPN is a human interactive account (not a service principal/automation) and that no sanctioned VPN/SWG egresses via these AWS ranges; review the sign-in's app, prior sign-in locations, and whether the user received a RecruitTrap lure (UC1). 2) Contain: Revoke all refresh/session tokens (revokeSignInSessions), force password reset, and require phishing-resistant re-registration; block the source IP. 3) Hunt: Check AuditLogs for security-info/MFA method additions, new OAuth consent grants, and inbox-forwarding rules created after this sign-in, and review mailbox/SharePoint access from the same session.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"   // MFA satisfied — AiTM relay hallmark
| where ClientAppUsed == "Browser"
| where IsGuestUser == false
| where ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "3.80.0.0/12","34.192.0.0/10","35.152.0.0/13","44.192.0.0/11","52.0.0.0/11","54.144.0.0/12","18.204.0.0/14","100.24.0.0/13")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0                              // successful auth
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (14618, 16509)     // Amazon-02 / Amazon.com (EC2 hosting)
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"   // AiTM relay: MFA was completed
| where ClientAppUsed == "Browser"
| where UserType != "Guest"
| extend Ctry = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), City = tostring(LocationDetails.city)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Ctry, City, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HoneyMyte Defender exclusion for fake 'Microsoft\Windows Defender' path via WMIC MSFT_MpPreference AIInstallation High
Hunts the CoolClient pre-deployment step where PlugX adds a Microsoft Defender folder/file exclusion for the actor-created fake C:\Program Files\Microsoft\Windows Defender directory and its renamed sideloader defender.exe, using wmic MSFT_MpPreference call Add ExclusionPath. This is the exact evasion command shown verbatim in the article and is not a generic exclusion-add. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim article command (wmic /Namespace:\\Root\Microsoft\Windows\Defender ... MSFT_MpPreference call Add ExclusionPath) targeting the fake 'Microsoft\Windows Defender' dir — a path no legitimate admin excludes. Cross-checked against Securelist and The Hacker News which both describe the fake-Defender-dir + exclusion combo. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/mustang-panda-adds-signed-windows.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit EDR migration playbooks that script Add-MpPreference exclusions (but those rarely use wmic MSFT_MpPreference)
  • Software vendors' installers self-excluding their own install dir (different path, not Microsoft\Windows Defender)
  • Sysadmin performance troubleshooting excluding a real Program Files subfolder
  • Security-product deployment tools staging under Program Files
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"Program Files\Windows Defender", "ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender") and not ProcessCommandLine has @"Program Files\Microsoft\Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ExclusionPath value points at Program Files\Microsoft\Windows Defender (not the legit Program Files\Windows Defender); pull the parent process — CoolClient stages this via a PlugX/loader, so an unusual parent is a strong TP signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the malicious Defender exclusion (Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath), and preserve the fake directory for forensics before deletion. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for defender.exe (renamed Sangfor Sang.exe) sideloading libngs.dll, a schtasks 'Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service' task, and the msagent.sys driver service.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wmic.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "MSFT_MpPreference"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("MSFT_MpPreference", "ExclusionPath")
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "wmic.exe" or CommandLine has "MSFT_MpPreference"
| where CommandLine has "MSFT_MpPreference" and CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where CommandLine has @"Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CoolClient sideloader staging: xcopy clones legit Windows Defender folder into fake Microsoft\Windows Defender dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the CoolClient environment-setup step that mirrors the real C:\Program Files\Windows Defender folder into the actor-created C:\Program Files\Microsoft\Windows Defender directory via xcopy, to make the fake install location look authentic before dropping the renamed Sangfor sideloader. The source→destination pairing of two Defender paths is the distinctive tell. Rationale: Uses the verbatim xcopy staging command (xcopy "...\Windows Defender\*" "...\Microsoft\Windows Defender") — a source/destination pair of two Defender folders that only occurs when an actor is faking a Defender install location. Corroborated by Securelist's fake-Defender-directory description. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/mustang-panda-adds-signed-windows.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/imaging scripts snapshotting the Defender directory (rare; usually robocopy of full drives, not just Defender)
  • IT migration copying Program Files during OS upgrade
  • Antivirus removal/repair tooling relocating Defender files
  • Admin manually copying Defender logs for support cases
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the destination path is Program Files\Microsoft\Windows Defender and inspect what files landed there (look for libngs.dll, libsrapc.dll, loadcert.ini, cert.ini, time.ini). 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the fake directory tree; capture the renamed defender.exe (should carry Sangfor version metadata). 3) Hunt: pivot to the schtasks persistence task and the wmic Defender-exclusion command on the same host, and sweep other endpoints for the same destination path.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "xcopy.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"Windows Defender" and ProcessCommandLine has @"Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "xcopy.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Windows Defender" and CommandLine has @"Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CoolClient persistence: schtasks onstart SYSTEM task masquerading as 'Windows Defender ATP Service' running defender.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the CoolClient persistence mechanism — a scheduled task named '\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service' created onstart, running as SYSTEM, whose action launches the renamed Sangfor sideloader defender.exe from the fake Defender directory. The task name + SYSTEM + defender.exe action triad is article-specific. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim schtasks command from the article (/sc onstart /tn '\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service' /tr defender.exe /ru system). The legit Defender ATP service is 'Sense', so a scheduled task by this name running defender.exe is a masquerade. Corroborated by The Hacker News and Securelist. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/honeymyte-coolclient-driver-rootkit/121028/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/mustang-panda-adds-signed-windows.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft-shipped Defender scheduled tasks under \Microsoft\Windows\Windows Defender\ (those run MpCmdRun.exe/MsMpEng.exe, NOT defender.exe)
  • EDR/MDR onboarding scripts creating Defender-related tasks (different action binary)
  • GPO-deployed maintenance tasks referencing Defender
  • Admin renaming/recreating a real Defender task during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun.exe", "MsMpEng.exe", "NisSrv.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task with `schtasks /query /tn "...Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service" /xml` and confirm the /tr action points to defender.exe in Program Files\Microsoft\Windows Defender (a real Defender task never runs defender.exe). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the task, and quarantine the fake defender.exe + libngs.dll. 3) Hunt: check for the msagent.sys driver service, UAC-bypass artifacts, and injection into synchost.exe; sweep the fleet for the identical task name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "defender.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
