Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] JWR phishing-kit landing: victim beacon + ws-worker.js load in web proxy telemetry · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Curiouser and Curiouser
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JWR real-time exfil & operator WebSocket channel (the_final_interface / addCvv / webSocket/QT)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
JWR phishing-kit landing: victim beacon + ws-worker.js load in web proxy telemetry AIDelivery High
Hunts managed endpoints reaching a JWR (a.k.a. 'The Outsider' variant) real-time phishing page, identified by the kit's bespoke arrival-beacon REST endpoints (api/open/addclick, api/open/getSyncSettings) and its isolated WebSocket worker script (static/js/ws-worker.js). These URI paths are unique to the JWR client engine and indicate a user landed on a live smishing checkout/login lure. Rationale: Anchored on JWR's bespoke client-engine URI paths from the full Talos write-up (api/open/addclick beacon, api/open/getSyncSettings config pull, static/js/ws-worker.js). No legitimate application uses this exact combination, so a single hit is high-fidelity. Requires proxy/SWG or MDE network telemetry that carries the full URL path (TLS-inspected). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/dissecting-the-jwr-phishing-framework/ • https://cybernews.com/news/cisco-talos-paypal-apple-phishing-kit-jwr/ • https://cyberpress.org/jwr-phaas-hits-banking/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst manually detonating the JWR kit from a corporate host
  • Automated URL-sandbox / detonation service (URLScan, Any.Run, Hybrid Analysis) egress captured by proxy
  • SOC-operated honeypot or phishing-simulation platform reusing kit code
  • Under HTTPS without TLS inspection the RemoteUrl may only carry the hostname, causing silent misses (not FPs) rather than noise
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-analysis") or InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("svc-urlscan","threatintel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DeviceName/SrcIpAddr is a corporate user browser session and extract the full host + URL; pivot to the impersonated brand (toll authority, postal/courier) in the domain. 2) Contain: block the domain/IP at the proxy and web gateway, isolate nothing yet but force a session-token reset and step-up MFA for the affected user; warn the user they hit a live phishing page. 3) Hunt: search all proxy logs for the same host and for the JWR exfil endpoints (api/open/the_final_interface, api/open/addCvv, webSocket/QT/) to determine whether data was actually submitted.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(api/open/(addclick|getSyncSettings)|static/js/ws-worker\.js)"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)(api/open/(addclick|getSyncSettings)|static/js/ws-worker\.js)"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DvcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JWR Phishing Kit Arrival Beacon and Worker Script in Proxy Logs
id: 6f3c2a71-0b4e-4c9a-9a5c-2d8e7f1b4c30
description: Detects a web request to JWR phishing framework arrival-beacon endpoints or its isolated WebSocket worker script, indicating a user landed on a live JWR/The-Outsider smishing lure page.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/dissecting-the-jwr-phishing-framework/
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/curiouser-and-curiouser/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/18
tags:

  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1204.001

  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'api/open/addclick'
      - 'api/open/getSyncSettings'
      - 'static/js/ws-worker.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*api/open/addclick*" OR Web.url="*api/open/getSyncSettings*" OR Web.url="*static/js/ws-worker.js*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

JWR real-time exfil & operator WebSocket channel (the_final_interface / addCvv / webSocket/QT) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the active data-theft stage of the JWR phishing framework: the AES-CTR-encrypted exfiltration POSTs to api/open/the_final_interface and api/open/addCvv, the HTTP long-poll fallback api/open/pollInstruction, and the operator-driven live WebSocket channel webSocket/QT/. A hit means card data, credentials, 2FA codes and device fingerprints were streamed to the operator in real time. Rationale: Uses the JWR exfiltration/C2 URI paths documented by Talos (api/open/the_final_interface and api/open/addCvv exfil POSTs, api/open/pollInstruction fallback, webSocket/QT/ operator channel). These strings are unique to the kit and represent data actually leaving the victim, making this the highest-severity JWR pivot. Depends on proxy/SWG telemetry carrying full URL paths. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/dissecting-the-jwr-phishing-framework/ • https://mallory.ai/stories/019ffacf-5b1f-75ac-969e-39f1e4b434c0 • https://cyberpress.org/jwr-phaas-hits-banking/
ATT&CKT1557 T1111 T1056.003 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher/analyst submitting fake data into the live kit during investigation
  • Automated sandbox detonation interacting with kit forms
  • Phishing-simulation vendor reusing captured kit code internally
  • Generic app coincidentally using a 'webSocket/QT/' path (rare; the api/open/* endpoints are far more specific and should be weighted higher)
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-analysis") or InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("svc-urlscan","threatintel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat as data-loss — identify the user and confirm the browser session hit an exfil endpoint (the_final_interface/addCvv = card+CVV submitted; to_2fa/to_pin operator commands imply MFA relay). Determine what the user entered. 2) Contain: reset the user's credentials and revoke all active sessions/tokens (stolen device fingerprints + session tokens bypass conditional access), enroll phishing-resistant FIDO2 MFA, and notify the card issuer/fraud team if payment data was entered. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination host/IP across all users, correlate back to the UC1 arrival beacon to scope every victim, and check identity logs for anomalous sign-ins reusing the harvested session.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(api/open/(the_final_interface|addCvv|pollInstruction)|webSocket/QT/)"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)(api/open/(the_final_interface|addCvv|pollInstruction)|webSocket/QT/)"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DvcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PATCHCORD delivery via TMS_AfghanTelecom.exe Inno Setup installer / known hashes · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New PATCHCORD Backdoor Targets Afghan Telecom and Indian Critical Infrastructure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PATCHCORD 'BeaconBrowserHijack' Run-key persistence (APT36) · [LLM] PATCHCORD/SHEETCORD browser shortcut (.lnk) hijack write · [LLM] SHEETCORD VBS Startup-folder persistence drop · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PATCHCORD C2 beacon to appstoore.solutions / 46.30.188.13:8080 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
PATCHCORD 'BeaconBrowserHijack' Run-key persistence (APT36) AIInstallation High
Hunts the PATCHCORD backdoor writing its executable path to a HKCU Run value literally named 'BeaconBrowserHijack', the marker it uses to flag an already-compromised host and gate its browser-shortcut hijacking routine. The value name is unique to this APT36/Transparent Tribe implant, giving a near-zero-FP persistence signal. Rationale: The value name 'BeaconBrowserHijack' under CurrentVersion\Run is a literal, implant-specific string with no legitimate use; cross-checked against Acronis TRU report and gbhackers/scworld write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/patchcord-new-malware-cluster-targets-afghan-telecom-and-south-asian-critical-infrastructure/ • https://gbhackers.com/patchcord-infrastructure-hosts-supershell/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-patchcord-backdoor-targets-afghan-telecom-and-south-asian-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None realistically expected — the value name is a unique implant marker
  • A red-team/purple-team emulation of PATCHCORD replaying the exact IOC
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a monitored lab reporting into production tenant
  • Threat-intel platform writing IOC test artifacts to a canary host
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full Run key value data (InitiatingProcessCommandLine/RegistryValueData) to recover the on-disk PATCHCORD executable path and hash it. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, delete the Run value and the referenced binary, and force-reset any browser shortcuts (see the .lnk hijack UC). 3) Hunt: Sweep for outbound connections to 46.30.188.13:8080 / appstoore.solutions and for the same Run value across the estate; check for SHEETCORD Startup-folder VBS on peers.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "BeaconBrowserHijack"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "BeaconBrowserHijack"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PATCHCORD/SHEETCORD browser shortcut (.lnk) hijack write AIInstallation Medium
Hunts modification or creation of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Opera or Vivaldi .lnk shortcuts by a process that is not a legitimate browser/installer. PATCHCORD rewrites these shortcut targets to its own executable (passing the real browser path as an argument) so the implant launches first on every browser click while preserving the user experience. Rationale: Article states PATCHCORD/SHEETCORD hijack browser .lnk shortcuts across six named browsers, rewriting the target to the implant while keeping the real browser path as an argument; excluding legit browser/updater writers isolates the malicious rewrite. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/patchcord-new-malware-cluster-targets-afghan-telecom-and-south-asian-critical-infrastructure/ • https://gbhackers.com/patchcord-infrastructure-hosts-supershell/
ATT&CKT1547.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate browser auto-update repinning a Start Menu/Taskbar shortcut
  • Third-party software-deployment tools (SCCM/Intune/PDQ) recreating browser shortcuts
  • User-profile roaming or shortcut-repair utilities rewriting .lnk files
  • Enterprise browser-management agents enforcing default-browser policy
  • Backup/restore tooling recreating shortcuts on a reimaged host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read the .lnk target with an offline parser — PATCHCORD points the target at a non-browser exe and moves the true browser path into Arguments; confirm the writing process and its folder. 2) Contain: Isolate host, restore clean browser shortcuts, quarantine the referenced executable, and check for the BeaconBrowserHijack Run value. 3) Hunt: Search for the same non-browser writer process across the fleet and correlate to C2 beacons to 46.30.188.13:8080.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where FileName has_any ("Chrome","Edge","Firefox","Brave","Opera","Vivaldi")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe","googleupdate.exe","update.exe","operasetup.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "lnk"
| where TargetFileName has_any ("Chrome","Edge","Firefox","Brave","Opera","Vivaldi")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","update.exe","OperaSetup.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PATCHCORD C2 beacon to appstoore.solutions / 46.30.188.13:8080 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on outbound connections or DNS lookups to the PATCHCORD single-C2 infrastructure — IP 46.30.188.13 (TCP 8080) and the hard-coded domains appstoore.solutions and the SHEETCORD delivery domain nic-support.site. These are the campaign's confirmed check-in endpoints. Rationale: 46.30.188.13:8080 and appstoore.solutions are the confirmed single-C2 endpoint (corroborated by gbhackers/scworld); nic-support.site is the SHEETCORD/NIC-impersonation delivery domain from the article's IOC set. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/patchcord-infrastructure-hosts-supershell/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-patchcord-backdoor-targets-afghan-telecom-and-south-asian-infrastructure • https://securityaffairs.com/197266/intelligence/apt36-suspected-in-patchcord-espionage-campaign-using-google-sheets-c2.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners/sandboxes in your estate proactively connecting to the IOC
  • Security researchers validating the IOC from a corporate egress IP
  • A shared-hosting IP reallocation later serving benign content (validate WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • Passive DNS/monitoring appliances resolving the domain for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify InitiatingProcessFileName/folder for the connection — PATCHCORD runs from a user-writable path and often has a browser passed as an argument; capture the binary. 2) Contain: Block 46.30.188.13 and the two domains at the proxy/firewall/EDR and isolate connecting hosts. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the offending process hash and check for the BeaconBrowserHijack Run value, hijacked browser .lnk files, and SHEETCORD Startup VBS on the same and neighbouring hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "46.30.188.13"
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("appstoore.solutions","nic-support.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "46.30.188.13"
    or Url has_any ("appstoore.solutions","nic-support.site")
    or DstDomain has_any ("appstoore.solutions","nic-support.site")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstDomain, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PATCHCORD delivery via TMS_AfghanTelecom.exe Inno Setup installer / known hashes AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on execution or drop of the PATCHCORD delivery chain — the Inno Setup installer TMS_AfghanTelecom.exe (from Telecom_TMS.zip, an Afghan Telecom Transport Management System lure) and the five campaign SHA256 hashes for PATCHCORD/SHEETCORD components. Rationale: Telecom_TMS.zip → TMS_AfghanTelecom.exe (Inno Setup) is the named PATCHCORD delivery artifact impersonating Afghan Telecom's Transport Management System, and the five SHA256 values are the article's pre-extracted campaign hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/patchcord-new-malware-cluster-targets-afghan-telecom-and-south-asian-critical-infrastructure/ • https://securitybrief.co.uk/story/apt36-linked-malware-cluster-targets-south-asia-telecoms
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected for the hashes — they are attributed malware samples
  • AV/EDR quarantine already firing on the same file generating a file-event echo
  • Malware-analysis lab detonating the sample and reporting to the production tenant
  • Filename collision on a benign in-house 'TMS' tool (validate by hash/signer before escalating)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the hash against the IOC list and capture parent process, download source (FileOriginUrl), and user. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, quarantine the installer and any dropped PATCHCORD/SHEETCORD binary, and reset the affected user's browser shortcuts + Run key. 3) Hunt: Search mail/proxy for Telecom_TMS.zip and nic-support.site deliveries, and sweep for C2 to 46.30.188.13:8080 and the BeaconBrowserHijack persistence marker.

| order by Timestamp desc

SHEETCORD VBS Startup-folder persistence drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a .vbs file created in the Windows Startup folder — the persistence mechanism SHEETCORD uses to relaunch its Go backdoor at logon (it then runs commands via PowerShell and beacons over the Google Sheets API). A VBScript planted in Startup by a non-standard process is a high-signal SHEETCORD/APT36 indicator. Rationale: Article states SHEETCORD 'uses the Windows Startup folder to establish persistence using a Visual Basic Script'; a .vbs written to the Startup path is rare in benign estates and directly matches this behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/197266/intelligence/apt36-suspected-in-patchcord-espionage-campaign-using-google-sheets-c2.html • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/patchcord-new-malware-cluster-targets-afghan-telecom-and-south-asian-critical-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately deploy a logon .vbs to Startup
  • IT logon-automation scripts (drive mapping, printer setup) staged via Startup VBS
  • Software installers that add a VBScript launcher to Startup
  • User-created automation placed in the Startup folder
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read the .vbs contents — SHEETCORD's script relaunches its backdoor and drives PowerShell; capture the process it invokes and any googleapis/Sheets references. 2) Contain: Isolate host, remove the Startup .vbs and referenced payload, and check for hijacked browser shortcuts + BeaconBrowserHijack Run value. 3) Hunt: Look for wscript.exe/cscript.exe or PowerShell child processes reaching sheets.googleapis.com and for nic-support.site delivery on the host and its peers.

| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where FileName endswith ".vbs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "vbs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-6387")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-6387")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

falsepositives:

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/

    - attack.t1027

    selection_image:

            - 'FromBase64String'

            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'

            - '-ep bypass'

    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:

      cross-shell escaping
level: high

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cf7184c0dfe882dc6e3016f16e4ede32b75d7648f83d6f4f87eb6a703be7b8d6", "1774e15e8eb96eb89bc03cb4768fc0620e10c09c5f795297f36dcc2aa5d9dd94", "ea0934472121848b80455581d289ce4480b1e5cc05678c1b90ecfc465b5ec350", "5e17360d32e9b272bb7e1b97c8e4dca34622ec9ce08fd240fe2758cc3f67dc4a", "378484112b4e837d3850b5b0802fc509202c232bb124d6944a59fe66525ba668"]);

macOS ClickFix: Terminal spawns shell decoding Base64 / curl-pipe payload AIDelivery High
Hunts the AmnesiaStealer initial-access step where a counterfeit GitHub 'Download for macOS' page tricks the victim into pasting a Base64-encoded command into Terminal, which decodes to a curl-to-shell dropper. Targets Terminal/iTerm parenting bash/sh/zsh/curl that either base64-decodes inline or pipes a remote fetch straight into a shell. Rationale: Uses the article's specific delivery chain (fake GitHub 'Download for macOS' + ClickFix Base64-into-Terminal → curl-to-shell dropper) pivoting on the Terminal→shell parent/child relationship, which is abnormal for pasted one-liners. Cross-checked Jamf and SecurityWeek. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://www.securityweek.com/amnesiastealer-macos-malware-steals-data-controls-browser-sessions/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-infostealer-spread-clickfix/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer pasting an install script (e.g. Homebrew 'curl ... | bash') into Terminal
  • IT automation onboarding scripts run interactively
  • Legitimate base64-encoded config snippets decoded during troubleshooting
  • Security researchers detonating samples in Terminal
  • CI/dotfile bootstrap commands executed by power users
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("brew.sh","raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew","get.docker.com","sh.rustup.rs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the Base64/inspect the curl URL; check whether the remote host resolves to known-good software vendors vs freshly-registered infra. 2) Contain: if the URL is unknown/malicious, isolate the host, kill the shell/child processes, and block the domain at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a follow-on password-protected ZIP download, a first-stage Mach-O in /tmp, dscl authonly / security unlock-keychain activity, and a new /Library/LaunchDaemons plist.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Terminal","iTerm2","iTerm")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","curl")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "base64" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-d","-D","--decode"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("| bash","| sh","| zsh","|bash","|sh","|zsh"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Terminal","iTerm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","curl")
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "base64" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-d","--decode"))
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("| bash","| sh","|bash","|sh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS captured-password validation via dscl authonly + keychain unlock with cleartext password AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts AmnesiaStealer's credential-validation and reuse chain: the fake installer prompt captures the system password, validates it against the local directory service with `dscl . -authonly`, then reuses it via `security unlock-keychain -p <password>` (cleartext on the command line). Both invocations from a non-login context are strong stealer signals. Rationale: Targets the article's exact tradecraft: password captured via a fake installer prompt, validated with dscl against the local directory service, then piped into security unlock-keychain -p. `-p` placing the password inline is highly abnormal for interactive users. Corroborated by Jamf and CSO Online. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4210464/new-macos-malware-turns-stolen-browsers-into-attacker-controlled-sessions.html
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1059.004 T1056.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM/automation scripts unlocking a keychain non-interactively for cert deployment
  • Admin scripting user authentication checks with dscl authonly
  • Jamf/Munki management workflows that unlock login keychains
  • Developer scripts automating code-signing that unlock keychains
  • Break-glass IT remediation on a locked account
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/Library/Application Support/JAMF" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jamf","munki","managedsoftwareupdate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process/path (a shell from /tmp or a random-named Mach-O is malicious; MDM daemons are usually benign) and whether the password appears in cleartext. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force a password reset for the affected user — assume the system password is compromised and reused across the chain. 3) Hunt: search the same host for cleartext password files (pwd, ~/.pwd), sudo -S usage, Chrome Safe Storage keychain reads, and outbound traffic to the C2.

| where (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "security" and ProcessCommandLine has "unlock-keychain" and ProcessCommandLine has "-p")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("loginwindow","login")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName =~ "dscl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (ActingProcessName =~ "security" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "unlock-keychain" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-p")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS browser 'Safe Storage' master-key theft via security find-generic-password AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts AmnesiaStealer reading the Chromium 'Safe Storage' master key out of the login keychain to decrypt saved cookies/logins. Detects the `security find-generic-password` CLI querying a '<Browser> Safe Storage' service, which browsers themselves never do (they use the Keychain API, not the CLI). Rationale: The article states the stealer reads the 'Chrome Safe Storage' password from the Keychain to recover Chromium master keys across 16 browsers. The `security find-generic-password ... Safe Storage` CLI invocation is a near-zero-legit-use, high-fidelity string. Confirmed by Jamf and SecurityWeek write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://www.securityweek.com/amnesiastealer-macos-malware-steals-data-controls-browser-sessions/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1555.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher manually extracting a browser key for DFIR
  • Red-team/pentest tooling (e.g. chrome cookie decrypt scripts) during authorized engagements
  • A password-manager migration utility reading browser stores
  • Developer debugging Chromium encryption locally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/Applications/" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("security","login")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/binary path and hash; a random-named Mach-O in /tmp or a shell child confirms malice. 2) Contain: isolate the host, invalidate/rotate the user's browser-synced credentials and session cookies, and force reauth on high-value SaaS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the /tmp staging directory (25 random alphanumeric chars), cookie/Login Data file access across Chromium profiles, and headless-browser CDP launches (the remote_stream stage).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "security"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "find-generic-password"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Safe Storage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "security"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "find-generic-password"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "Safe Storage"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS root LaunchDaemon persistence dropped by untrusted process (Apple crash-reporter impersonation) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts AmnesiaStealer's persistence: a root LaunchDaemon plist written into /Library/LaunchDaemons that impersonates Apple's crash-reporting service. Flags new/modified plists in that directory created by a process running from /tmp or user-writable staging paths, or with a crash-reporter-themed name. Rationale: The article states persistence is via a root LaunchDaemon that impersonates Apple's crash-reporting service. Legit LaunchDaemons are installed by pkg installers/MDM, not shells or /tmp binaries — so the initiating-process pivot plus the crash-reporter naming is what makes this article-specific. Corroborated by Jamf. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/amnesiastealer-macos-malware/
ATT&CKT1543.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installer pkgs deploying daemons (usually via installd, not a shell)
  • MDM (Jamf/Intune) pushing management LaunchDaemons
  • Homebrew services writing daemons via brew
  • Developer manually installing a daemon with a launchd helper
  • Backup/AV agents registering their own crash-reporter helpers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("installd","package_script_service","jamf","munki") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/Library/Application Support/JAMF"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the plist contents (ProgramArguments / RunAtLoad) and the initiating process — a shell or /tmp Mach-O writing it is malicious; installd/jamf is usually benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, unload the daemon (launchctl bootout), and remove the plist and referenced payload. 3) Hunt: correlate with the ClickFix Terminal execution, dscl/keychain credential access, and C2 beacons to scope the full infection on this and sibling hosts.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath startswith "/Library/LaunchDaemons/"
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Users/Shared/","/var/folders/")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript")
    or FileName has_any ("crash","Crash","report")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/Library/LaunchDaemons/"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".plist"
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","osascript") or TargetFileName has_any ("crash","report")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
